pattern_name: Kyber/ML-KEM Message Bit Decoding vs Compiler-Introduced Branch (Inverted)
variant_desc: Canonical Kyber message-bit decode `mask = -((msg[i]>>j)&1); r[8i+j] = mask & 1665;` -- LLVM trunk at -O1+ produces bt/jae/mov, leaking the bit via timing (slow) -> volatile-barrier-defended formulation that preserves the constant-time AND (fast) (variant 2: seed=44, n_scale=1.5x)
source_citation: Schneider et al. 'When Compilers Break Constant-Time' arXiv:2410.13489 (2024) Example 3; LLVM RFC __builtin_ct_select (Trail of Bits, 2024); PQShield 'Clangover' key-recovery attack on Kyber (2024).
novelty_rationale: INVERTED-FRAMING pattern, third of the CT triplet (HO-SR-4/5/6).  The 'slow' version is the canonical Kyber message-decode loop -- the exact code structure used in the reference Kyber implementation, recommended by NIST PQC reviewers, and reviewed by formal-CT tools that examine the SOURCE.  At -O1 and higher LLVM trunk recognizes the (bit ? 1665 : 0) idiom in `mask & 1665` with `mask = -bit` and rewrites into `bt + jae + mov` -- a branch on the message bit.  The PQShield Clangover attack (2024) exploits exactly this leak to recover Kyber session keys from ML-KEM decapsulation timing.  The 'fast' version uses a volatile barrier per iteration to keep the compiler from collapsing the mask into a select.  SPEED IS NOT THE METRIC: when LLVM 22's __builtin_ct_select intrinsic lands, that's the proper fix; until then, the volatile barrier is the portable defense.  correct=1 is the success metric.
